Verify by Doing: Co-Evolving Agent Execution and Evaluation without External Feedback

Yitong Lin1,2 *  Jianda Chen1 *  Yihao Hu1  Pan Wang1  Hang Wang1  Zhihao Wen1  Xiaoxue Ren2  Wei Wu1

1Ant International  2Zhejiang University

1 Introduction

Agent self-improvement depends on feedback that identifies successful attempts and guides updates to the procedures that produce them. At test time, agents can update their workflows or harnesses while keeping model weights fixed (Agrawal et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026), or use additional inference to generate and check more candidates (Snell et al., 2025; Brown et al., 2024). Both strategies depend on reliable feedback about whether the task has been completed. Beyond standardized benchmarks, reference answers and task completion signals may be unavailable, leaving the task request and observations from environment interaction as the main basis for verification.

This setting creates two coupled challenges: inferring task success from incomplete observations, and improving the agent when the resulting feedback may itself be incomplete. The budget example in Figure 1 illustrates why both matter: finding expected labels does not establish task completion, while generating more outputs under the same checks can preserve the same blind spots. This motivates active verification and adaptation of the verification procedure.

Existing methods address parts of these challenges. Tool-based critique can acquire additional observations (Gou et al., 2024), and retrospective diagnosis and preference history can guide updates to actor procedures (Pan et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Nie et al., 2026), but they do not update the verification procedure itself.

Incomplete verification can leave blind spots unresolved and misguide later adaptation (Wang et al., 2026a). Red Queen Gödel Machine jointly evolves agents and evaluators, using held-out ground truth to guide Evaluator replacement (Iacob et al., 2026). We study within-task adaptation where execution and verification evolve without external feedback from benchmark scores or labeled references.

We introduce Verify by Doing (VbD), which couples task execution with active verification. The Actor executes the task through an editable harness of instructions, skills, and working checks, while the Evaluator uses its own harness to inspect artifacts and environment state, recording satisfied, violated, and unresolved requirements. These findings ground preferences between task results and guide updates to both harnesses. Updating the verification procedure changes how this internal signal is produced, while requirements remain fixed.

After initialization, VbD tests retained and proposed Actor harnesses in the task environment (Figure 2). Each trial produces a candidate comprising an execution record, resulting state, and response or deliverable. Proposed Evaluators are reviewed against the retained version on the same candidates, comparing the evidential support and applicable criteria in their reports. The retained Evaluator’s findings guide output selection, while Actor adoption separately requires support for the proposed harness’s own fresh output. An Editor uses the findings, comparison decisions, and task history to propose further updates to either or both harnesses.

VbD makes three contributions:

  • •

    Active verification: verify by doing. Tool-based inspections gather evidence of task completion from artifacts and environment state.

  • •

    Evidence-driven harness co-evolution. Shared findings guide Actor and Evaluator harness updates within a single task.

  • •

    Comparative review and separate retention. Trials and report comparisons support separate decisions for Evaluator adoption, candidate selection, and Actor retention.

Across AutomationBench, τ3\tau^{3} Banking, and selected GDPval tasks (Patwardhan et al., 2025), VbD achieves the highest overall scores among the compared methods without external feedback on two backbones. Ablations support the contributions of active verification and Evaluator evolution, with positive mean gains on all three task sets. Holding BoN candidates fixed, the retained Evaluator improves pass rate and partial credit over the initial Evaluator, demonstrating better selection from the same candidate outputs. Case studies connect verification findings to execution improvements and selection of earlier successful candidates, while revealing remaining errors in evidence interpretation.

2 Related Work

Improving agent procedures.

Agent improvement methods differ in what they update and how feedback guides those updates. DSPy optimizes modular language-model pipelines, while AFlow searches code-represented workflows (Khattab et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). Voyager accumulates executable skills through environment feedback (Wang et al., 2023). Self-Refine and Reflexion improve outputs or later behavior (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023). GEPA evolves prompts, while DGM, HGM, and Hyperagents edit agent programs or improvement procedures (Agrawal et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026c). Self-Harness accepts edits using regression tests (Zhang et al., 2026a); ModularRSI combines program checks, overfitting review, and execution checks (Wu et al., 2026). Several methods adapt harnesses without labeled validation signals. RHO diagnoses past rollouts and selects harnesses for future tasks using a fixed self-preference ranking procedure (Pan et al., 2026). RHI revises a task-specific textual harness from pairwise preference history under a fixed evaluation prompt (Lee et al., 2026); TTHE edits executable harnesses from unlabeled traces (Nie et al., 2026). In contrast, VbD uses verification findings to update both Actor and Evaluator harnesses.

Obtaining evidence for judgment.

Judging task completion can require observations beyond the Actor’s trace. ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions that gather external information (Yao et al., 2023). CRITIC uses tools to critique outputs, Self-RAG learns retrieval and critique decisions, and LATS combines environment feedback with search (Gou et al., 2024; Asai et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024). Agent-as-a-Judge inspects artifacts against requirements, while VAGEN actively probes graphical interface state (Zhuge et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2026). The Verification Horizon studies informative verification as generation changes; AIChilles searches for workloads exposing regressions (Wang et al., 2026a; Zhou et al., 2026). Studies of intrinsic self-correction report failures without external feedback (Huang et al., 2024), while ProCo improves correction through structured condition verification (Wu et al., 2024b). VbD carries inspection findings into later rounds as proposed changes to both execution and verification.

Co-evolving execution and evaluation.

Process supervision trains reward models with human feedback on intermediate reasoning steps (Lightman et al., 2024). Other training approaches couple generation with learned rewards or feedback on judgments (Yuan et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024a); related work studies rubric learning and prover–verifier interaction (Ding et al., 2026; Kirchner et al., 2024). At the program level, RQGM co-evolves agents and evaluators through controlled utility evolution: evaluation remains fixed within each search stage and changes at qualified boundaries (Iacob et al., 2026). Its shared workspaces also permit edits affecting both roles. Double Ratchet selects evolving metrics with an anchored reference set (Zhang et al., 2026d). VbD uses active verification to couple execution and verification updates within a task, without external feedback. Comparative review evaluates evolving feedback procedures before they guide output selection and Actor retention decisions separately.

3 Problem Setting

We study agent improvement within a task xx, given its request, materials, and permitted tools. Each Actor candidate links an execution record, resulting state, and response or deliverable to its generating harness. Benchmark outcomes, official rubrics, and expert outputs are reserved for offline scoring.

Actor harness HH and Evaluator harness Φ\Phi contain instructions, working rubrics, and skills. Rubrics express checks against public requirements: Actor rubrics guide execution and self-checks; Evaluator rubrics guide assessment. Skills specify execution or verification procedures. HH also includes persistent check plans, distinct from temporary trial questions. Model weights, task requirements, permissions, editor, selector, and reviewer instructions, eligibility, and acceptance rules remain fixed.

The retained state includes an incumbent candidate zz, candidate set 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and history 𝒟\mathcal{D}. The incumbent need not come from the current Actor. Harnesses and history reset between tasks; the final output is frozen before scoring.

4 Verify by Doing

VbD addresses the two challenges in Section 1 by making verification both active and adaptable. Inspection supplies evidence for judging current outputs; the same findings guide changes to how the Actor executes and how the Evaluator checks completion. Because both procedures evolve, VbD reviews verification changes before selection and evaluates Actor changes through fresh trials.

Initialization inspects two attempts from the initial Actor and selects an incumbent without adopting updates. The editor prepares proposals if another round remains. Subsequent rounds follow Figure 2: Actor Trials, Agentic Evaluation, Comparative Selection, and Harness Co-evolution. A tilde denotes a proposal; a superscript ++ denotes retained state.

4.1 Actor Trials

A verification finding identifies a potential improvement, but the proposed harness must be tested through execution. Following harness optimization (Pan et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026), Step 1 runs the current Actor HH and proposed Actor H~\widetilde{H} to produce fresh candidates aa and bb. Both receive the same temporary checks; only the proposal uses persistent edits. This exposes both Actors to the current verification concerns while testing the proposed execution procedure. Temporary checks expire after the round unless reconsidered. Without a proposal, both attempts use HH.

Each candidate preserves its execution record, resulting state, and response or deliverable for subsequent verification. We append the candidates to 𝒢\mathcal{G} and record their generating harnesses. This link matters because an updated Evaluator may select an earlier output: selecting that output provides no trial evidence for adopting the proposed Actor. Fresh trials instead provide execution evidence for the separate retention decision in Section 4.3.

4.2 Agentic Evaluation

To judge completion from incomplete observations, Step 2 gathers evidence about the effects of execution. Each Evaluator independently inspects a common pool ℬ\mathcal{B}, locating relevant state or artifacts and executing checks for unresolved requirements. Workbook cell reads, for example, expose relationships left untested by header checks (Figure 1). Findings take the form

ℱΦ​(ℬ)={(ci,qi,oi,fi)}i=1m,\mathcal{F}_{\Phi}(\mathcal{B})=\{(c_{i},q_{i},o_{i},f_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m}, (1)

where each of the mm findings records a candidate ci∈ℬc_{i}\in\mathcal{B}, proposition qiq_{i}, observations and sources oio_{i}, and scoped assessment fif_{i} with uncertainty. Payer attribution requires linking a value to its source record. Figure 2 distinguishes Field, Relation, Aggregate, and Task scopes.

A fixed selector Π\Pi interprets these findings against the request:

d=Π⁡(x,ℬ,ℱΦ​(ℬ)).d=\Pi\bigl(x,\mathcal{B},\mathcal{F}_{\Phi}(\mathcal{B})\bigr). (2)

Record dd names a candidate and distinguishes supported preferences, ties, unresolved judgments, and fallbacks. Its preference supplies the internal signal; the findings guide execution and verification updates. Updating Φ\Phi changes how evidence is acquired and assessed while the task xx and selector Π\Pi stay fixed.

4.3 Comparative Selection

Incomplete checks can favor outputs that miss requirements (Skalse et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2023). Adapting verification can reveal missed requirements but also changes the basis for judging Actor improvement. Step 3 therefore tests the proposed Evaluator on common candidates, uses the retained procedure to select an output, and requires support for the Actor’s fresh output before adoption.

Evaluator adoption.

A fixed reviewer tests whether the proposed verification procedure produces better-supported findings on the same candidates. It compares evidential support, criterion applicability, and counterexamples in the two reports. Both orders are reviewed to reduce sensitivity to position bias (Zheng et al., 2023). Let VEV_{E} indicate a completed valid trial and v1,v2v_{1},v_{2} be votes mapped to Evaluator identities:

Φ+={Φ~,VE∧v1=v2=Φ~,Φ,otherwise.\Phi^{+}=\begin{cases}\widetilde{\Phi},&V_{E}\land v_{1}=v_{2}=\widetilde{\Phi},\\ \Phi,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (3)

Without a tested proposal, VEV_{E} is false and the current Evaluator is retained.

Output selection.

The retained Evaluator supports selection from the eligible candidates 𝒞⊆𝒢\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{G}, with further inspection as needed. Qualification and selection may use different candidate sets (Appendix B.1):

d+\displaystyle d^{+} =Π⁡(x,𝒞,ℱΦ+​(𝒞)),\displaystyle=\Pi\bigl(x,\mathcal{C},\mathcal{F}_{\Phi^{+}}(\mathcal{C})\bigr), (4)
z+\displaystyle z^{+} =out⁡(d+).\displaystyle=\operatorname{out}(d^{+}).

Here out\operatorname{out} returns the named candidate, including a fallback representative. Improved verification can select an earlier successful output even when fresh attempts fail.

Actor retention.

Actor adoption requires support for the proposal’s own fresh candidate. Let VAV_{A} denote a valid trial of a changed Actor. Indicators s1,s2s_{1},s_{2} record strict support in the initial comparison (or candidate-set selection) and the subsequent incumbent comparison, each requiring agreement in both presentation orders:

H+={H~,VA∧(z+=b)∧s1∧s2,H,otherwise.H^{+}=\begin{cases}\widetilde{H},&V_{A}\land(z^{+}=b)\land s_{1}\land s_{2},\\ H,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (5)

Condition z+=bz^{+}=b requires selection of the proposal’s own output; s1∧s2s_{1}\land s_{2} excludes fallback choices. Selecting an earlier output leaves the Actor unchanged. This rule holds across main experiments and ablations (Appendix B.1).

4.4 Harness Co-evolution

To carry a verification finding into later attempts, Step 4 translates it into a proposed change to execution, verification, or both. The fixed editor ℒedit\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{edit}} specifies an expected effect and a corresponding check for the next trial. Retrieving a supposedly unavailable contact sheet (Figure 2), for example, supplies an Actor retrieval instruction and an Evaluator check for future unavailability claims. The same observation can therefore provide both execution guidance and a verification procedure.

After appending attempts, proposals, and decisions to history 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+}, the editor prepares proposals if another round remains:

(H~next,Φ~next)=ℒedit​(x,H+,Φ+,𝒟+).(\widetilde{H}_{\mathrm{next}},\widetilde{\Phi}_{\mathrm{next}})=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{edit}}(x,H^{+},\Phi^{+},\mathcal{D}^{+}). (6)

History preserves rejected trials and observation sources to inform later proposals (Lee et al., 2026); unchanged components receive no update. Steps 1–3 evaluate these proposals, and their findings guide subsequent edits. Inspection, adaptation, and review connect Actor behavior, Evaluator checks, and the retention of changes. After the final round, VbD returns the selected output (Algorithm 1).

5 Experiments

The results support VbD’s central premise: execution and its guiding verification procedures benefit from evolving together. Overall gains, fixed-candidate selection, and ablations support this design. Update decisions distinguish output selection from Actor retention; cases and behavioral changes connect verification findings to reusable execution guidance and checks.

5.1 Experimental Setup

The three benchmarks require different evidence of task completion. AutomationBench evaluates workflow execution through saved application state on 600 tasks across six domains (Shepard and Salimans, 2026). τ3\tau^{3} Banking tests whether dialogue and actions satisfy policy on 97 tasks (Shi et al., 2026). GDPval assesses professional deliverables (Patwardhan et al., 2025); we use 133 tasks supported by our text and document tools. Appendix B.2 gives the GDPval selection criteria.

Here, external feedback refers to benchmark scores or reference labels; the internal signal is the preference inferred from verification evidence (Equation 2). We score final selected outputs by pass rate on AutomationBench and Banking, and mean rubric quality on GDPval. Official checks, rubrics, and expert outputs are reserved for offline scoring, except for the reference with external feedback. GDPval’s rubric score differs from its official expert pairwise win rate.

The main experiments use DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 for all task roles with frozen weights. Offline grading with language models uses GPT-5.6-sol with xhigh reasoning effort. All iterative methods use two Actor executions per round for three rounds, then freeze selected outputs for offline scoring. VbD’s main experiments and ablations share comparative Actor acceptance (Equation 5); eligibility and budgets remain fixed within each task. Main tables report mean and sample standard deviation (SD) across three runs. Appendix B.9 details aggregation and uncertainty.

5.2 Baselines

Base model makes one attempt (Pass@1); best-of-NN (BoN) selects from six candidates using VbD’s initial Evaluator. On AutomationBench, self-preference (SP) follows VbD’s schedule with both harnesses fixed.

Among adaptive methods, Huxley–Gödel Machine (HGM) searches Actor policies (Wang et al., 2026b), Retrospective Harness Optimization (RHO) diagnoses earlier executions (Pan et al., 2026), and Recursive Harness Self-Improvement (RHI) uses preference history (Lee et al., 2026). Red Queen Gödel Machine (RQGM) co-evolves agents and evaluators (Iacob et al., 2026); our adaptation preserves staged search and best-belief replacement. Evaluation is fixed within each stage; replacement renews dependent statistics.

All methods include instructions, skills, and working rubrics; evolving baselines reset per task. Permitted task observations replace HGM’s benchmark utility and RQGM’s labeled anchors (Appendix B.3). Configurations appear in Tables 4 and 6, and inference costs in Figure 3. The unranked external feedback reference (†\dagger) runs HGM search under fixed benchmark scoring.

5.3 RQ1: Task Performance at Test Time

Does co-evolving execution and verification improve task performance? VbD achieves the highest overall scores among the compared methods without external feedback on all three task sets (Tables 1–3). The gains span workflow execution, interactions requiring policy compliance, and professional deliverables, supporting the value of improving execution and verification together.

The gains extend to professional deliverables: VbD leads all nine GDPval sectors, with 82.4% overall rubric quality versus RQGM’s 80.1%. On AutomationBench, selected outputs also satisfy more individual requirements, as shown by higher partial credit (Appendix B.7).

The evidence differs across tasks, but verification serves a common purpose: inspection findings connect the Actor’s actions to observable task requirements. This grounds adaptation in evidence about completion while keeping the task requirements fixed, allowing the same findings to guide both execution and verification.

AutomationBench pass rate rises from 30.0% to 34.3% and then 37.0% across rounds (Figure 3). These gains accompany additional inference for verification, editing, review, and selection. VbD’s second-round mean already exceeds RQGM’s final 33.7% at a lower cumulative token cost. Each plotted method generates six Actor candidates over its full schedule. VbD finishes 5.6 percentage points below the external feedback reference. Overall gains persist with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Appendix B.5).

5.4 RQ2: Internal Signal for Co-evolution

How does the internal signal support selection and Actor updates? We assess Actor update decisions within each method’s own evolution runs and Evaluator selection on a shared, fixed BoN candidate pool.

We label an Actor proposal as an improvement or regression by comparing its output’s offline partial credit with the output it was evaluated against, using valid, non-tied pairs. TP and FP count accepted improvements and regressions; TN counts rejected regressions. We report

TNR=TNTN+FP,Precision=TPTP+FP.\mathrm{TNR}=\frac{\mathrm{TN}}{\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FP}},\qquad\mathrm{Precision}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}}.

VbD rejects 89.3% of observed regressions compared with 71.2% for RQGM, while maintaining similar precision (77.6% versus 77.0%; Figure 4(a)). This advantage of 18.1 percentage points in regression rejection accompanies an update acceptance rate similar to those of HGM and RQGM (Appendix B.9).

Incomplete verification can overlook successful outputs already in the candidate pool. To isolate selection, we compare VbD’s and RQGM’s final Evaluators with BoN’s initial Evaluator on six fixed BoN outputs per task (Figure 4(b); Appendix B.4). VbD exceeds both BoN and RQGM, improving pass rate by 4.6 percentage points and partial credit by 2.4 over BoN. Since the available outputs are unchanged, these gains come from selecting better work already in the pool. Marketing088 illustrates the change in feedback: consistently applying the response-scope requirement gives the selector a basis to distinguish similar recorded actions and select an existing passing output (Appendix C.7).

5.5 RQ3: Active Verification and Evaluator Evolution

What do acquiring evidence and adapting verification each contribute? The variant without active verification assesses existing traces without new inspections while retaining harness evolution. The variant without Evaluator evolution inspects candidates with fixed Evaluator instructions, rubrics, and skills while the Actor evolves. Tasks, initial harnesses, base model, three-round schedule, and strict Actor acceptance rule are shared.

Both removals lower the mean score on every task set while Actor evolution remains active (Tables 1–3). On AutomationBench, removing active verification lowers the mean by 2.7 percentage points, and freezing the Evaluator lowers it by 1.6. Banking and GDPval follow the same pattern.

The ablations distinguish acquiring evidence from retaining verification lessons. A frozen Evaluator still gathers observations, but its instructions, rubrics, and skills remain unchanged. Its lower scores support carrying lessons forward: missed requirements motivate persistent checks, and successful inspections supply reusable procedures. Active verification expands the evidence for current judgments, while Evaluator evolution adapts future checks under fixed task requirements. Actor evolution cannot fully compensate.

5.6 RQ4: Co-evolution in Practice

How does a verification finding improve both execution and feedback? The cases trace how findings become reusable actions and checks through two paths: exposing a missed requirement and discovering an operation the Actor can reuse.

In Sales063, initial attempts omit customer-record updates and violate a reply restriction (Figure 7). Verification accepts an untested claim that the service is unavailable and overlooks the restriction. VbD adds an Actor skill for reply scope and a matching Evaluator criterion; the next attempt completes the updates and satisfies the restriction. HGM and RQGM complete the main actions but retain replies naming excluded attendees. The case shows how a missed requirement becomes guidance for both execution and assessment.

In Marketing015, the Evaluator retrieves a contact sheet through an operation the Actors missed. The successful retrieval becomes an Actor instruction and an Evaluator availability check (Figure 2); distribution then succeeds. The initial Evaluator also recognizes success. Verification supplies more than a verdict here: it reveals an action the Actor can reuse and a check for future claims that a resource is unavailable.

Other cases show why output selection and Actor adoption are separate decisions. Support091 recovers an earlier passing output despite failed fresh attempts. Sales047 selects a passing new output but withholds the Actor update because the final comparison lacks strict support (Appendix C.8). Verification can still misinterpret evidence: Finance024 treats a file timestamp as a business date and selects a failing output (Appendix C.9).

Actor behavior complements these cases: attempts containing state verification rise from 20.4% in Round 1 to 25.3% in Round 3 (Appendix D.1). The cases trace how findings become Actor checks; the aggregate trend is consistent with this transfer from verification to execution.

6 Conclusion

VbD co-evolves Actor and Evaluator harnesses through active verification, comparative review, and separate retention. Across three task sets and two backbones, it achieves the highest overall scores among the compared methods without external feedback. Ablations and fixed-candidate selection support improving execution alongside the verification procedure that supplies the internal signal.

Together, these findings explain the value of evolving verification alongside task execution. Active verification supplies evidence, co-evolution turns findings into execution guidance and reusable checks, and separate retention distinguishes successful outputs from supported updates. Task requirements and model weights stay fixed; adaptation changes how the agent executes, checks completion, and carries verification findings into subsequent attempts. More broadly, VbD suggests that test-time agent improvement can progress beyond choosing among existing behaviors by evolving the procedures that produce and evaluate feedback.

Limitations

VbD relies on observable evidence and model-based judgments. The Actor, Evaluator, and reviewer may share errors in interpreting evidence, so active verification and comparative review cannot eliminate incorrect selections or updates (Wang et al., 2026a).

Repeated trials require states or artifacts that can be isolated and inspected. As with replay-based adaptation (Pan et al., 2026), irreversible actions and environments that cannot be reset limit direct application. Delayed effects or inaccessible state may also escape verification.

Our experiments evaluate three-round adaptation within individual tasks. Transfer across tasks and sustained improvement over longer evolution remain untested. Additional execution, verification, and harness revision incur inference and tool-use costs; deployment latency also depends on environment response times.

Ethical Considerations

VbD studies tool-using agents on benchmark tasks. Errors in execution or verification can lead to unintended messages, incorrect record updates, or misleading deliverables. Harness adaptation retains fixed task requirements and tool permissions. Deployment in real environments should enforce these permissions, protect sensitive information in execution logs and artifacts, and require human oversight for consequential actions. Access to personal or business data should be limited to the authorized task, and use or redistribution of benchmark materials and derived artifacts should respect the applicable licenses and access conditions.

Appendix A Complete Evolution Procedure

VbD uses verification findings to guide both harnesses, while retaining outputs and updates through separate decisions. Algorithm 1 specifies how these decisions fit into one co-evolution round after initialization.

The retained state comprises Actor harness HH, Evaluator harness Φ\Phi, incumbent zz, candidate set 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and history 𝒟\mathcal{D}. A tilde denotes a proposal; a superscript ++ denotes the retained state after the round. Actor state includes persistent check plans. Without an Evaluator proposal, Φ+=Φ\Phi^{+}=\Phi; without an Actor proposal, both fresh attempts use HH.

A.1 Evidence, Selection, and Updates

Both Evaluators inspect a common candidate pool with their respective harnesses fixed during each inquiry. Findings identify the candidate, proposition, observations, and assessment (Equation 1). The selector interprets these findings against the task requirements, including observed defects and unresolved requirements. A supported finding may establish a defect, such as excessive page count; its consequence for the task determines the preference, rather than the number of supported findings.

Evaluator adoption requires a valid trial and agreement in both review orders. The retained Evaluator supports output selection; Actor adoption additionally requires strict support for the proposed Actor’s own output (Equation 5). Fallback selections leave the Actor unchanged.

The editor uses findings and trial history, including rejected proposals, to update either or both harnesses. Each proposal connects an observed gap to an expected change in execution or verification. Task requirements, tool permissions, model weights, controller instructions, and acceptance rules remain fixed. VbD returns the final selected output, then resets its harnesses and history.

Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results

Unless otherwise stated, empirical analyses use DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 under the settings in Tables 4–5. We use offline benchmark scores to assess the complete loop, selection by the evolved Evaluator, and Actor retention. Ablations test evidence acquisition and persistent verification updates. Only the external feedback reference uses these scores during evolution (Appendix B.8).

B.1 Execution Schedule

All iterative methods use three rounds with two Actor executions per round, totaling six attempts per task per run. For VbD, Round 1 runs the initial Actor twice to initialize the candidate pool and select an incumbent; no harness update is adopted in this round. Rounds 2–3 test current and proposed Actors using proposals prepared in the preceding round. SP uses the same schedule and budgets with fixed harnesses.

To keep execution and assessment aligned, each candidate records its generating harness and resulting state or deliverable. Evaluators inspect a common pool, and selection uses the retained Evaluator’s findings, with further inspection as needed. An earlier candidate remains available through its saved output and state.

Comparison stages and candidate sets.

Evaluator qualification uses the common review pool ℬ\mathcal{B}; output selection uses the eligible pool 𝒞⊆𝒢\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{G}, which may include earlier attempts. Candidate eligibility is fixed throughout evolution and excludes offline task-success labels. Reused evidence retains its candidate identity and observation scope. The main experiments and ablations apply the retention rules in Equations 3 and 5, with the comparison procedure described in Appendix A.

After the retention decisions, the editor proposes changes to instructions, rubrics, skills, or persistent check plans and specifies how to test them. Both fresh Actors receive the same temporary checks; only the proposed Actor receives persistent edits. Temporary checks expire after the round unless reconsidered. History records component sources, executed checks, and retention decisions. Changes to persistent Actor check plans count as Actor proposals even when the other harness text is unchanged.

Budget boundaries.

Operations are bounded by their assigned response limits and remaining task allowance. When no response remains, execution terminates with an error and produces no completed prediction.

B.2 Tasks, Scoring, and Configuration

The AutomationBench public set (v1.0.5) contains 600 tasks, with 100 in each of six workflow domains. Banking contains 97 tasks, with success requiring both the correct final database state and the required communication actions. These task sets evaluate completed interactions; GDPval extends the comparison to professional deliverables.

GDPval selection covers tasks supported by our text and document tools: spreadsheet contents, document structure, measurable formatting, and editable chart data. We select 133 of the 220 public gold tasks, covering nine sectors and 41 occupations.

Selection follows task requirements and reference availability, without filtering by method scores. All methods use the same task IDs and complete rubrics.

For evaluation, AutomationBench and τ3\tau^{3} Banking score each method’s final selected output. Pass rate uses the full task denominator; unresolved grades receive no pass credit. Base model makes one attempt, while the other methods submit their selected candidate. All task-local harnesses reset between tasks.

The single-attempt control uses the first BoN candidate, including failed attempts. GPT-5.6-sol with xhigh reasoning effort grades deliverables using official rubrics and expert artifacts. Task scores apply criterion weights and retain penalties; sector scores average their tasks, and overall scores average all 133 tasks within each run. We report the mean and sample SD across three runs. These are local rubric scores, distinct from official expert pairwise win rates. Rubrics and expert artifacts are used for offline scope review and scoring, except in the external feedback reference.

Shared settings and model configurations.

Table 4 lists the shared execution limits and evolution protocol; Table 5 gives parameter counts and model-specific inference settings for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. Full role specifications appear in Appendix E.

The shared loop accesses application state in AutomationBench, policy prerequisites and exceptions in Banking, and file contents and calculations in GDPval (Figure 5). Actor harnesses guide the requested actions; Evaluator harnesses inspect their effects using the permitted task interfaces.

B.3 Baseline Adaptations

Table 6 summarizes the evaluated configurations; Table 7 compares the original formulations. HGM uses a utility posterior for Actor search and final selection [Wang et al., 2026b]. Our budget of six attempts limits runtime and token costs, but may reduce HGM and RQGM’s tree search to an effectively linear sequence of updates.

RHO originally improves a harness for future tasks by diagnosing grouped rollouts on a coreset of past tasks. It proposes harness changes from these diagnoses and accepts the best proposal only when its mean pairwise self-preference is strictly positive [Pan et al., 2026]. Our adaptation retains retrospective diagnosis and self-preference-guided Actor updates within the current task. Earlier executions of that task supply the diagnostic history in place of a cross-task coreset, and subsequent attempts test the revised Actor within the six-execution budget. The Evaluator remains fixed throughout adaptation.

RHI originally revises a textual harness using accumulated pairwise preferences between successive executions, with a fixed Evaluator; its stopping criterion aggregates improvement across tasks [Lee et al., 2026]. Our adaptation retains task-specific instruction revision from harness and preference history. Each round executes two candidates within the shared six-execution budget, using task-local feedback and a fixed Evaluator. Table 11 reports the RHI acceptance statistics.

Both adaptations use the execution and response limits in Table 4. Harnesses and histories reset between tasks, and benchmark scores remain reserved for offline evaluation.

RQGM additionally changes the Evaluator between search stages. In the original method, evaluation remains fixed within each search stage; replacement uses the highest best-belief score on labeled anchors, optionally augmented with an adversarial objective, and ties retain the incumbent [Iacob et al., 2026]. Our task-local adaptation preserves this structure and replacement rule but estimates utility from permitted task observations. Report comparisons supply evidence for that estimate. Replacement excludes statistics dependent on the displaced Evaluator from subsequent search, while earlier outputs remain available for reassessment.

VbD instead reviews Evaluator proposals within each co-evolution trial and applies the separate retention rules in Equations 3 and 5.

RQGM utility estimation.

For each Evaluator–candidate pair, the fixed assessment procedure records whether the report’s material findings follow from observed evidence and applicable task requirements. Supported assessments contribute to SS; evidenced incorrect claims, inapplicable criteria, or material omissions contribute to FF. Insufficient evidence contributes to neither count. Each pair contributes at most one observation; reassessment updates that observation. A report correctly identifying a failed Actor attempt can therefore receive positive utility. We compute the replacement score as

BBϵ​(e)=Qϵ​[Beta⁡(1+Se,1+Fe)].\mathrm{BB}_{\epsilon}(e)=Q_{\epsilon}\!\left[\operatorname{Beta}(1+S_{e},1+F_{e})\right]. (7)

Here QϵQ_{\epsilon} denotes the ϵ\epsilon-quantile, with ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05 by default. At a stage boundary, the highest-scoring observed Evaluator replaces the incumbent only on a strict improvement; ties retain the incumbent, and an unobserved alternative cannot displace it.

B.4 Evaluator Selection Quality

To isolate selection quality, we hold Actor outputs fixed. We compare BoN’s initial Evaluator with RQGM’s and VbD’s final retained Evaluators on the same six BoN candidates per task. Each Evaluator uses its own inspection procedure to select one output on each of the 600 AutomationBench tasks. VbD uses the Evaluator retained by Equation 3, keeping the initial version if no update is adopted. All selectors use both presentation orders; disagreement is resolved by selecting the smallest original candidate identifier. We report pass rate and partial credit averaged across three runs.

Pass rate is 35.8% for VbD’s Evaluator, 33.4% for RQGM’s Evaluator, and 31.2% for the BoN baseline (Figure 4(b)). Partial credit is 69.8%, 68.5%, and 67.4%, respectively. VbD’s evolved Evaluator exceeds BoN by 4.6 percentage points in pass rate and 2.4 in partial credit.

B.5 Evaluation Across Model Backbones

With Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, VbD reaches 48.4% on AutomationBench, 57.4% on Banking, and 84.7% rubric quality on GDPval, leading the compared methods without external feedback in all three overall scores (Tables 8–10). On AutomationBench, it exceeds RQGM by 3.3 percentage points overall and achieves the highest mean score in all six domains among methods without external feedback. It also leads in all nine GDPval sectors. The gains hold across both backbones.

The Qwen3.8-Flash-Next evaluation uses the shared protocol and model settings in Tables 4–5. Baseline schedules follow Section 5.2. Offline scoring uses the same task sets and three-run aggregation as the DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 evaluation.

B.6 Evolution Trajectories and Inference Cost

Figure 3 pairs each round’s selected-output pass rate with cumulative tokens per task. Cost includes Actor execution, harness editing, evaluation, comparative review, and output selection; it excludes offline grading and the fixed-candidate Evaluator analysis. Each method is plotted at its incurred cost, with final pass rates and SDs from Table 1. All compared methods generate six Actor candidates per task (BoN-6: six one-shot samples; VbD: two per round over three rounds).

VbD gains 4.3 percentage points from Round 1 to Round 2 and a further 2.7 in Round 3, reaching 37.0%. Its second-round mean of 34.3% already exceeds RQGM’s final 33.7% at a lower plotted cumulative cost.

B.7 Partial Task Completion

Pass rate credits a task only when all scored checks pass. AutomationBench also provides partial credit, the fraction of scored assertions satisfied for each task [Shepard and Salimans, 2026]. Averaging these fractions reveals progress that binary task completion can conceal.

Figure 6 shows VbD increasing from 66.35% to 70.26%, a gain of 3.91 percentage points. RHO increases from 62.83% to 66.83%. VbD exceeds BoN from Round 2 onward and finishes 1.63 percentage points above the strongest baseline, RQGM. This complements the results on pass rate: later outputs satisfy a larger fraction of scored requirements.

B.8 Evolution with External Feedback

The external feedback reference uses HGM to evolve the Actor under fixed model weights, with benchmark scores guiding updates and output selection. AutomationBench and τ3\tau^{3} Banking supply outcome checks; GDPval supplies local rubric scores. VbD and other baselines use these scores only offline.

Tables 1–3 compare the same task sets. The reference generates its own candidates, whereas an oracle-selection bound requires a shared candidate pool [Brown et al., 2024].

B.9 Statistical Reporting

Aggregation and uncertainty.

Main result tables report mean ±\pm sample SD across three evaluation runs. Overall scores are computed within each run before aggregation; SD is in percentage points, and rounding is applied only for display. Mean differences are reported in percentage points. Behavioral bootstrap intervals summarize variation across tasks using the procedures in Appendix D.3.

For GDPval, Tables 3 and 10 use the same 133 tasks and sector weights. Within each run, Overall averages task scores, equivalently weighting sector means by sector task counts. Its mean and sample SD are computed across the three run-level Overall scores using unrounded values; each reported entry is then rounded to one decimal place.

Update gating.

We assess Actor update decisions over the three-round evolution schedule for each method, using offline partial-credit scores for the recorded proposal–comparison pairs (Table 11). A proposal is positive if its output scores higher than its recorded comparison output, and negative if it scores lower. TP counts accepted improvements, FP counts accepted regressions, and TN counts rejected regressions, using valid, non-tied offline partial-credit pairs. The gate makes its decisions from public evidence; offline scores label the outcomes for this analysis.

For each method, acceptance rate is Na/NpN_{a}/N_{p}, where NpN_{p} and NaN_{a} count all proposed and accepted updates. TNR is TN/(TN+FP)\mathrm{TN}/(\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FP}), and precision is TP/(TP+FP)\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}); both use valid, non-tied score pairs. All three metrics are percentages.

These measures describe different aspects of retention. Acceptance rate gives its frequency, TNR measures rejection of observed regressions, and precision measures the fraction of improvements among accepted updates. VbD’s higher TNR accompanies similar precision and acceptance rates to RQGM. The observed distinction is therefore most pronounced in filtering regressions. This analysis characterizes the complete retention procedure, while the case histories show why an output can be selected without accepting its producing Actor.

Appendix C Case Studies of Harness Co-evolution

The following recorded cases use DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and trace how verification findings change execution instructions, evaluation criteria, and output selection. They also document updates that are rejected and findings that are misinterpreted, showing where additional evidence does not lead to a better decision.

C.1 Budget Verification

The budget task requires correct payer attribution, consistent totals, and tax-adjusted net revenue (Figure 1). The initial Evaluator checks labels and headers but leaves the numerical relationships untested. A proposed skill inspects expense and revenue cells through four table probes. Both review orders favor this procedure, while the earlier workbook remains selected.

The figure’s nine sum checks and seven net checks are offline recomputations from the returned cells that establish arithmetic consistency for those cells. Payer attribution requires comparing the workbook’s assignments with source records.

C.2 Grant Spending

The grant task classifies spending relative to elapsed project time. An updated skill uses Python to recompute elapsed time and apply the task’s thresholds to the recorded spending percentage. For the sampled award, about 16.5% of the period has elapsed while 99.6% of the funds are spent, satisfying the rapid-spending condition. This check supports retaining the workbook, although later checks in the episode fail to execute (Listing E.3).

C.3 Press Release Distribution

In Marketing015, both initial Actors fail to read the contact spreadsheet and send no task emails. The Evaluator retrieves the rows through an alternative operation, prompting an Actor retrieval instruction and an Evaluator skill for checking resource availability. In Round 2, the proposed Actor follows the instruction to send the release to three eligible outlets and a summary to the team. Inspection checks a sent release and the summary; both harness updates are adopted, and the passing output remains selected in Round 3. The Actor follows the revised instructions without explicitly loading a skill, and the initial Evaluator also recognizes success. The update therefore supplies a missing retrieval procedure and a check on claims of resource unavailability (Listings E.3–E.3).

C.4 Webinar Follow-up

Sales063 requires personalized follow-up emails, updated customer records, and a final reply describing only completed actions. Figure 7 and Table 12 trace this task’s execution across three rounds.

In Round 1, both initial attempts send follow-up emails but omit updates to customer records and discuss excluded attendees. The selected attempt claims the record service is unavailable without testing it. The Evaluator accepts that explanation and misses the reply restriction. The editor proposes a skill for checking the Actor’s final reply and a corresponding Evaluator rubric.

In Round 2, the proposed Actor loads the skill, updates the customer record and attendance, and reports only completed actions. Inspection finds the requested update in its saved state and no matching record in the earlier attempt. The proposed Evaluator checks both the saved state and reply scope, testing the earlier claim of service unavailability against observable results [Wang et al., 2026a]. Both updates are accepted, and the selected output passes offline scoring.

In Round 3, a further proposal tests service availability before declaring a limitation. It is not adopted, and the successful Round 2 output remains selected.

HGM and RQGM complete the customer-record updates and emails but retain replies that name excluded attendees. HGM checks the saved records and emails in Round 2 yet retains the reply “Not contacted (below threshold).” RQGM distinguishes the updated engagement threshold from a superseded rule and tests an Evaluator update concerning a deleted test lead. That trial produces no findings with stronger evidential support, so RQGM retains its Evaluator and earlier output. VbD’s paired updates instead incorporate the missed reply restriction into both execution guidance and assessment.

C.5 Supplier Strategy

The supplier task requests a two- to three-page strategy. An initial six-page preview prompts Actor instructions to shorten and check the draft and Evaluator instructions to inspect its rendered length. Both fresh previews show three pages; VbD selects the proposed Actor’s draft and adopts the proposed Evaluator.

HGM detects excessive length but retains a four-page draft. RQGM tests a stricter page-limit policy, but both Evaluators already detect the fresh drafts’ excess length. It therefore retains its Evaluator and earlier selected draft.

A common-renderer audit finds four pages for HGM, three for RQGM, and two for VbD (Figure 8); both RQGM and VbD meet the requested range. RQGM also claims that two domestic suppliers have been identified, whereas the supplied evidence concerns domestic capability. HGM and VbD describe the search as proposed work. VbD retains its draft and adopts another Evaluator update; some content requirements remain unresolved.

C.6 Evolving Verification of Earlier Attempts

In Support091, the Actor remains fixed while revised verification recovers an earlier successful output. The task requires consolidating duplicate tickets, sending notifications, and logging completed actions without mentioning untouched items in the reply. Round 2 finds no supported difference between the compared outputs and retains the initial selection. In Round 3, inspection revisits the same earlier pair and detects excluded-item narration in the initial output. An Evaluator update is adopted, and the passing Round 2 candidate is selected even though both fresh Round 3 attempts fail. Listings E.3–E.3 document the revised criterion and message reads.

In Tables 12 and 13, selected-output labels identify the generation round; a dash denotes no Evaluator proposal. Sales063 improves execution and assessment together, whereas Support091 improves selection while retaining the Actor.

C.7 Evolved Verification for Selection

Marketing088 tests whether revised verification can identify a successful output when candidate availability is fixed (Figure 9). All selectors receive the same six independently generated BoN outputs. The retained Evaluator selects a passing candidate in both presentation orders, addressing the incomplete-feedback problem described in Section 1.

The task requires invoicing overdue approved sponsors, applying Finance’s processing requirements, and updating the tracker; the final summary must list only acted-on items. Candidates A and B each record three invoice sends totaling $7,200, status updates, and a reconciliation email. A also lists five skipped sponsors and their exclusion reasons, whereas B reports completed actions without enumerating exclusions.

In the reversed presentation, the initial Evaluator finds no material difference among the most complete candidates on their recorded business effects. The retained Evaluator checks reply scope against the original instruction and distinguishes A from B in both orders. Its reversed-order inquiry also confirms B’s three updated tracker statuses. The reply check thus supplies a relevant distinction that the comparison of business effects alone misses.

Self-preference and the initial Evaluator each choose B in the forward order and A in the reversed order; the shared fallback rule resolves the disagreement to A. The retained Evaluator chooses B in both orders. Independent offline checks mark A as failing with 84.2% partial credit and B as passing with 100%. These labels are unavailable during selection.

C.8 Success without Actor Adoption

In the customer-health scoring task Sales047, a successful output is selected without adopting its Actor update (Figure 10). In Round 2, both nomination orders strictly favor the proposal for retrieving the scoring policy and verifying persisted updates. Both final comparisons declare equivalence: the reports acknowledge scores of 50 versus 35 but treat the difference as immaterial because both fall in the same health category. The proposal is selected, but the absence of strict final support blocks Actor adoption. Offline checks mark the proposal as passing and both the incumbent and fresh parent attempt as failing. The same passing output remains selected in Round 3.

C.9 Failure in Date Interpretation

In Finance024, the selected invoice report passes after Rounds 1–2 but fails after Round 3. The Evaluator substitutes the file’s write timestamp for the report’s business date, assigns all six invoices to the oldest overdue category, and selects a failing output over the passing incumbent. No harness update is adopted. The failure results from interpreting the observed timestamp as evidence of a different event.

Marketing015 and Sales063 trace findings into changes to both roles, whereas the budget case, Support091, and Marketing088 improve verification or selection of existing work. Sales047 shows that selecting a passing output need not lead to Actor adoption. The supplier and date cases limit what can be concluded from individual checks: a page count establishes length but not content coverage, and a file timestamp does not by itself establish the report’s business date.

Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution

Figures 11–12 and Table 14 analyze DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731; Figures 13–14 use Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. Skill loading records explicit use of evolved guidance, while Verify calls capture checks of action effects. These measurements connect the case studies to aggregate changes in Actor behavior.

D.1 Skill Use and Verification Behavior

For findings to improve execution, later Actors must use the guidance produced by harness evolution. The share of attempts loading skills rises from 0.0% in Round 1 to 23.1% in Round 3 (Table 14). This use of explicit guidance complements the cases in which a discovered operation or missed requirement becomes a reusable Actor skill.

Later rounds use fewer Search calls and more Verify calls. Attempts containing state verification rise from 20.4% to 25.3% between Rounds 1 and 3, while total calls per attempt fall from 63.8 to 54.6 (Table 14). Thus, more attempts include state checks even as the average execution uses fewer calls. Search decreases in every domain, while verification increases vary across domains (Figure 12).

The cross-method comparison with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next places VbD’s increased checking in context (Figure 13). HGM and RHI also reduce Search and Read, but their Verify frequency remains flat or decreases.

RQGM shows a smaller change in Verify, while RHO remains relatively stable across all three categories. VbD combines reduced Search with increased Verify, a direction also seen in the external feedback reference. This pattern is consistent with VbD’s design: verification findings guide both output assessment and checks performed during subsequent execution. Appendix D.3 details the measurements.

These observations connect the Actor side of VbD to the Evaluator results. On fixed candidates, the evolved Evaluator selects better outputs (Appendix B.4); in later executions, Actors use evolved skills and check state more often. The cases trace how shared findings link these changes, while the ablations support both acquiring evidence and retaining improved checks (Section 5.5). Together, these results support VbD’s central design: improve execution and the verification procedure that supplies its internal signal within the same task.

D.2 Task Outcome Visualization

The task projection displays Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outcomes on individual AutomationBench tasks. Figure 14 projects TF-IDF task descriptions using 50-dimensional TruncatedSVD, normalization, and t-SNE with PCA initialization and perplexity 35. Both panels share 200 tasks and coordinates; outcome labels determine display inclusion and annotations, while the projection uses task text. Orange highlights VbD successes missed by all six candidates from the external feedback reference. “Hard” and “Normal” are display labels for these highlighted tasks and their context.

D.3 Behavioral Measurement Protocol

For each method and backbone, we analyze both Actor executions per round on all 600 AutomationBench tasks across three runs, including failed attempts and rejected proposals. We average counts and attempt-level rates within tasks, then across tasks.

Table 15 extends RHO’s action categories [Pan et al., 2026] with explicit skill loading and other calls. Verify takes precedence over Read and Search.

Verify counts later read-backs of the same object after an action without an explicit error; source consultation and prerequisite checks remain Search or Read. All behavioral analyses use the same object-matching rule. Verification and skill-loading rates count attempts with at least one corresponding call.

Within-round trajectories.

In Figure 11, step kk counts tool calls within an attempt. The top row estimates the fraction of tasks with a passing selected output generated within kk calls, normalized to each round’s pass rate. These curves follow the selected output’s original execution, excluding discarded attempts and controller work.

The middle row reports mean calls per attempt per position in five-call bins; ended attempts contribute zero. The bottom row magnifies Verify on the same basis. Count changes use relative percentages; share and attempt-rate changes use percentage points.

Behavioral intervals resample tasks, retaining each task’s attempts and rounds together. Initial-to-final changes use within-task differences, and domain intervals resample within domains. Paired outcome comparisons retain all 600 tasks, with unresolved grades receiving no pass credit.

Appendix E Harness Specification

The harnesses express task requirements as procedures for execution and verification. Role instructions define how each procedure operates; recorded updates and executed checks show how an observed gap becomes guidance that the agent can use.

E.1 Role Policies and Verification

Listings E.3–E.3 give the Actor instructions, and Listing E.3 gives the Evaluator instructions. These accompany the task, working rubric, available skills and tools, and assigned checks. Tool availability follows the evaluated condition.

The Evaluator inspects unresolved requirements using the instructions and tools in Listings E.3–E.3. Returned observations guide further inquiry until completion or budget exhaustion.

Skills check delivered effects and rule applicability, including competing interpretations (Listings E.3–E.3). Both roles’ rubrics specify a criterion, a verification plan naming the needed observations, a falsifier identifying contrary evidence, and an unknown rule for unresolved evidence (Listings E.3–E.3).

E.2 Updates, Selection, and Recorded Use

The joint editor proposes changes and expected observations (Listing E.3). Listings E.3–E.3 specify Evaluator review and output preference; Appendix B.1 defines trials and retention.

In Marketing015, a successful lookup becomes an Actor retrieval instruction and an Evaluator availability check (Listings E.3–E.3). Support091 instead pairs an adopted content criterion with message reads that change selection between existing outputs (Listings E.3–E.3). Sales063 updates both roles around the reply restriction: an Actor skill checks reply scope and an Evaluator rubric assesses the same requirement (Listings E.3–E.3). Listing E.3 records the rationale and expected observations for that proposal.

Two further records show why verification must remain tied to a candidate’s own environment. Sales052 checks whether a policy was available and reads the delivered message before judging its omission (Listing E.3). Finance097 establishes that a newer status update was available to the candidate and checks the delivered journal; the observation precedes the skill adopted in the following round (Listing E.3). The listings preserve the requests, returned evidence, and retention decisions. Their Round 3 trials record no explicit skill loading; the observations describe the full Evaluator procedure.

E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks

For GDPval, the Actor creates and reopens deliverables; the Evaluator inspects their contents and native structure (Listings E.3–E.3).

Listings E.3–E.3 specify the verification skills adopted for numerical requirements, with an executed date-and-threshold check recorded in Listing E.3. The remaining examples reproduce executed programs for source coverage, native workbook structure, and numerical consistency (Listings E.3–E.3). Award reconciliation compares the complete qualifying ID set with the delivered workbook. Pivot inspection tests for native workbook components that displayed totals cannot establish. Capacity verification recomputes a recurrence over the entered demand and capacity. Each program is paired with its returned observation, so the reader can see both the checked property and the inputs on which the conclusion depends.
